Fractional hour concepts build from the hour unit: quarter-hour and half-hour are explicitly defined as 15 and 30 minutes relative to an hour. Hints reinforce hour hand identification on clocks. This demonstrates that hour is a foundational unit across the problem set.

Six samples explicitly present half-hour (30-minute) concepts. cd9ab15dffb62b187ff1 asks about lunch lasting half an hour; 5fba3bbf8c248173e41a and 3cd2d2a4b4aabbc2cefb ask about recess and story time lasting half an hour. Samples 7499971b786803da914e, 23c52f991f9c84a3b57d, and fcd0ddb28f814a5b884c present duration calculation problems where the interval is 30 minutes. Clock visuals show the minute hand at the 6-position (half-hour marker) with hints stating the long hand at 6 represents half past the hour. Half-hour equivalence to 30 minutes is made explicit in problem stems and options.

Only two samples explicitly address quarter-hour (15-minute) concepts, representing minimal coverage for a named competency element. Sample ff24e3f7564a16176ec2 asks about a break lasting a quarter of an hour (15 minutes) starting at 9:00. Sample 251a6ad4de14157610a6 asks about reading time lasting a quarter of an hour starting at 8:00. Both provide the minute equivalence (15 minutes) and use clock visuals showing the minute hand at the 3-position. While the two samples correctly execute quarter-hour concepts with appropriate scaffolding, the sparse representation (2 of 35 samples) compared to half-hour (6 samples) and hour-based duration problems (12+ samples) indicates underrepresentation despite being a named competency requirement.

Seven samples explicitly ask students to identify the day of the week from calendar visuals. d9113e76787866ca1193 asks about May 21, 2025; 8eb701b2d9aebbf2d869 asks about June 6; 6b957feeaa63811556da asks about October 10; 6dfa956416dc09363aa3 asks about June 21; 56e82086bbf0f0f30b1e asks about August 31; 3e0fdcfae651e3017259 asks about May 16; 492b80baaa5834bfded8 asks about October 14. These samples require reading calendar layouts, locating specific dates, and identifying ordinal positions within the week structure. Calendar visuals clearly label days (Sun, Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat) in order, providing the structural support needed for Grade 1 learners to understand days within weeks.

Ten samples address months: 3aa17e57ae386d9582d4 (March to May), 3d0fdafb47fcc8771b33 (May to July), b635b1309447cbdd1ef2 (May to September), 14207dcc88d8aa05a8ec (May to August), 2a2fdd54bc9804a91232 (September to November), 4c4112aefd320ea62b39 (February to May), b6f62b736ee963ac5ea0 (March to July), 06d5deeec5f8a90c9b6a (February to June), and 6c41fafb2faf71bcfa9b (July to September). Coverage is adequate in breadth, requiring month name recall and forward counting across calendar boundaries. However, three samples contain critical visual-text mismatches that undermine learning delivery: 3aa17e57 stem says March, visual shows September; 2a2fdd54 stem says September, visual shows March; 4c4112ae stem says February, visual shows April. These contradictions, paired with hints directing students to use the calendar, create contextual defects where students following instructions encounter the wrong reference month.
